title: The Polynomial Method and Alon's Theorem
content: Introduces Alon's Combinatorial Nullstellensatz (1999), a cornerstone of the polynomial method in combinatorics. The theorem states: if a multivariate polynomial $f$ over a field $F$ has a nonzero coefficient at a maximal-degree monomial $\prod x_i^{t_i}$ with $\deg f = \sum t_i$, then $f$ cannot vanish on any product grid $S_1 \times \cdots \times S_n$ where $|S_i| > t_i$. Applications include the Cauchy-Davenport theorem, Chevalley-Warning, permanent bounds, and the Alon-Tarsi theorem on list colorings.
mathContext: The Combinatorial Nullstellensatz works over arbitrary fields (not just algebraically closed), unlike Hilbert's Nullstellensatz from algebraic geometry. The name is an analogy: both concern when polynomials must have common zeros, but the combinatorial version gives explicit non-vanishing on product sets.

title: Single-Variable Non-Vanishing (Fully Proved)
content: Proves `exists_eval_ne_zero`: if $f \in F[x]$ is nonzero and $|S| > \deg(f)$, then some $s \in S$ satisfies $f(s) \ne 0$. The proof uses `Polynomial.card_roots_le_degree` from Mathlib: $f$ has at most $\deg(f)$ roots, so with $|S| > \deg(f)$ elements, at least one is not a root. The proof is by contradiction: assuming all $s \in S$ are roots gives $|S| \le |\text{roots}(f)| \le \deg(f)$, contradicting the hypothesis.
mathContext: This is the base case for the full Nullstellensatz. Over a field, a nonzero polynomial $f \in F[x]$ of degree $d$ has at most $d$ roots (by the factor theorem and degree counting). So if $|S| > d$, the pigeonhole principle gives $\exists s \in S: f(s) \ne 0$.

title: Grid Non-Vanishing Lemma (Axiomatized)
content: Axiomatizes the grid non-vanishing lemma: if $f \in F[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ is nonzero with $\deg_{x_i}(f) < |S_i|$ for each $i$, then $f$ does not vanish on $S_1 \times \cdots \times S_n$. The docstring outlines the inductive proof: viewing $f$ as a polynomial in $x_1$ with coefficients in $F[x_2, \ldots, x_n]$, if $f$ vanished on the grid, the single-variable case forces all coefficients to vanish on $S_2 \times \cdots \times S_n$, contradicting the induction hypothesis.
mathContext: Write $f = \sum_{j=0}^{d_1} c_j(x_2, \ldots, x_n) \cdot x_1^j$ with $d_1 = \deg_{x_1}(f) < |S_1|$. For each $(a_2, \ldots, a_n) \in S_2 \times \cdots \times S_n$, $g(x_1) = f(x_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$ has degree $\le d_1 < |S_1|$. If $g$ vanishes on $S_1$, then $g = 0$, so $c_j(a_2, \ldots, a_n) = 0$ for all $j$. Since this holds for all grid points, each $c_j$ vanishes on $S_2 \times \cdots \times S_n$, and by induction $c_j = 0$, so $f = 0$, contradiction.

title: Alon's Combinatorial Nullstellensatz (Axiomatized)
content: The main theorem: given $f$ with $\deg(f) = \sum t_i$ and nonzero coefficient at $\prod x_i^{t_i}$, and sets $S_i$ with $|S_i| > t_i$, there exists a point in $\prod S_i$ where $f$ does not vanish. The proof reduces to grid non-vanishing via polynomial division: reduce $f$ modulo $g_i(x_i) = \prod_{s \in S_i}(x_i - s)$ to get remainder $r$ with $\deg_{x_i}(r) < |S_i|$. The key insight: the target monomial $\prod x_i^{t_i}$ has degree $t_i < |S_i|$ in each variable, so it survives the reduction unchanged.
mathContext: The polynomial division step: $f \equiv r \pmod{g_1, \ldots, g_n}$ where $g_i = \prod_{s \in S_i}(x_i - s)$. Since $g_i$ vanishes on $S_i$, $f$ and $r$ agree on the grid. The monomial $\prod x_i^{t_i}$ has $\deg_{x_i} = t_i < |S_i| = \deg(g_i)$, so it is not reduced, preserving the nonzero coefficient. Thus $r \ne 0$ and grid non-vanishing applies.

title: ≥ t_i + 1 Variant (Proved from Axiom)
content: Restates the Combinatorial Nullstellensatz with $|S_i| \ge t_i + 1$ instead of $|S_i| > t_i$. The proof is a one-line reduction via `omega` converting $\ge t_i + 1$ to $> t_i$. This variant is sometimes more convenient in applications where set sizes are given as equalities.
mathContext: $|S_i| \ge t_i + 1 \Leftrightarrow |S_i| > t_i$ for natural numbers. The variant exists because applications sometimes express the condition as $|S_i| \ge t_i + 1$ (e.g., when $|S_i| = t_i + 1$ exactly, which is the tight case).

title: Uniform Grid Specialization (Proved from Axiom)
content: Specializes the Nullstellensatz to the case where all sets $S_i$ are the same set $S \subseteq F$: if $f \in F[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ has total degree $\sum t_i$ with nonzero leading monomial coefficient and $|S| > t_i$ for all $i$, then $f$ does not vanish on $S^n$. Proved by setting all $S_i = S$ in the main axiom.
mathContext: The uniform grid case is common in applications: e.g., in the Cauchy-Davenport theorem, one works with subsets of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, evaluating polynomials on $A^k$ for some $A \subseteq \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$.

title: Polynomial Method Framework and Proof Roadmap
content: Documents the polynomial method paradigm: to prove a combinatorial statement about a set $A$, construct a polynomial $f$ encoding the structure, then use algebraic properties (degree bounds, coefficient non-vanishing) to derive combinatorial conclusions. Lists four key applications: Cauchy-Davenport on sumsets, Chevalley-Warning on low-degree systems, permanent bounds, and the Alon-Tarsi theorem. The summary identifies the main gap for full formalization: multivariate polynomial division in Mathlib.
mathContext: The path to removing the `combinatorial_nullstellensatz` axiom requires: (1) MvPolynomial division modulo $g_i(x_i) = \prod_{s \in S_i}(x_i-s)$ one variable at a time, (2) degree bound preservation $\deg_{x_i}(r) < |S_i|$, and (3) coefficient preservation for monomials with $\deg_{x_i} < \deg(g_i)$.
